list.listitem: The diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) is made by establishing the occurrence of multiple episodes of neurologic dysfunction that are disseminated in time and location within the central nervous system (see ). C
Acute attacks (episodes of neurologic dysfunction lasting greater than 24 hours) should be treated with high-dose IV steroids for 3 to 5 days. A

Immunomodulatory medications such as monoclonal antibodies, interferons, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide, and glatiramer prevent relapses and slow disease progression in patients with relapsing remitting MS. Several monoclonal antibodies are effective for relapsing MS. Ocrelizumab has been shown to improve clinical outcome in patients with primary progressive MS, and tolebrutinib for secondary progressive MS. A
MS is both highly variable and unpredictable in its course. The majority of patients begin with relapsing-remitting MS and 50% ultimately convert to secondary progressive disease. B

background.definition: Multiple sclerosis is an inflammatory, presumably autoimmune disease of the central nervous system, usually characterized by relapsing and remitting focal neurologic symptoms.

list.listitem: In the U.S., the annual age and sex adjusted incidence is about 6 per 100,000 per year and is fairly stable.
MS most commonly presents in patients aged 20 to 40 years and has a 2:1 female to male ratio.

Administrative data from private health insurance, military, Medicare and Medicaid was used to estimate the prevalence of MS in different racial, gender, and ethnic groups in the US in 2010:
Black: 298/100,000 adults White: 375/100,000 adults Hispanic any race: 161/100,000 adults Non-Hispanic any race: 198/100,000 adults
Female to male ratio: 2.9 to 1
Second most common cause of acquired disability in the young.
Based on 1994 data, it cost an estimated $34,000 per patient per year. This translates to about $7 billion per year in the U.S. and an estimated lifetime cost of $2 million per patient.
The cost of caring for a single relapse in the U.S. is about $13,000, 70% of which is hospital-related cost.
Immunologic.

Genetic: Siblings of patients with MS have a 20- to 40-fold increased risk of developing MS. There is 2% to 5% concordance in non-identical twins or other siblings, and 20% to 30% concordance in identical twins. Recent genomic studies identified alleles of IL2RA and loci in the HLA-DRA gene as heritable risk factors.
Environmental: Populations living farther from the equator have a higher risk of acquiring MS.

In relapsing remitting MS, activation and inhibition of immunologic factors cause inflammatory demyelination and axonal injury. In progressive MS, there is ongoing axonal degeneration without significant inflammation.
Within an active MS lesion, the presence of inflammatory cells including lymphocytes and phagocytes, as well as immunoglobulins and complement, support an immunologic role in disease pathogenesis.
The higher prevalence seen with greater distance from the equator suggests that a pathogen exposure may trigger the autoimmune response.
Patients with multiple sclerosis should receive immunizations as recommended by the Centers for Disease Control. A
Patients with compromised pulmonary function (e.g., wheelchair bound, bed bound, etc.) should receive pneumococcal vaccination. C
The diagnosis of MS is made by establishing the occurrence of multiple episodes of neurologic dysfunction that are disseminated in time and location within the central nervous system (see ). C
The diagnosis is confirmed with gadolinium enhanced MRI of the brain and spine, the presence of oligoclonal bands in the CSF, and abnormal visual evoked potentials. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Optic neuritis accompanied by acute transverse myelitis; presence of neuromyelitis optica antibodies
Severe demyelination following viral illness; monophasic
MRI typically shows subcortical rather than periventricular lesions
Extra-neurologic manifestations common, abnormal autoimmune antibodies
Extra-neurologic manifestations; inflammatory cells in CSF; abnormal angiotensin converting enzyme levels
CSF positive for Lyme IgG, IgM
Progressive; non-enhancing periventricular lesions; immunocompromised patient; CSF + for JC virus
CSF cytology positive for abnormal cells
Neurologic exam inconsistent with symptoms; it is the most common alternate diagnosis

list.listitem: Please see for diagnostic criteria.
The term Clinically Isolated Syndrome (CIS) is used when a patient has their first attack of demyelinating disease but has not met the formal diagnostic criteria.
A relapse or exacerbation is defined as new or worsening neurologic deficit lasting over 24 hours in the absence of fever or other conditions that transiently increase MS symptoms.

Presenting symptoms and findings are highly variable and may not correlate with location of MRI lesions. Symptoms may include monocular visual loss (optic neuritis) with decreased color discrimination; acute/subacute onset of focal weakness or dysesthesia in extremities; ataxia; diplopia, or dysarthria (scanning speech) or other brainstem symptoms.
Other symptoms include Lhermitte's phenomenon (flexion of neck causes an electric shock sensation down the spine) and other sudden-onset sensory symptoms (such as trigeminal neuralgia).
Symptoms are typically exacerbated by heat (Uhtoff's phenomenon).
Mental status: signs of depression or anxiety; slurred or scanning speech.
Cranial nerves: visual loss, afferent pupillary defect, nystagmus, intranuclear ophthalmoplegia, facial numbness or weakness (including Bell's-palsy type facial asymmetry).
Motor: focal weakness including hemi-paresis or para-paresis, increased or asymmetric reflexes, upgoing toes on plantar reflex testing, increased muscle tone or spasticity.
Coordination: dysmetria on finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing, impaired rapid alternating movements, positive Romberg sign.
Sensory: loss of vibration, proprioception, or pinprick sensation; spinal cord sensory level.
Gait: evidence of paresis or ataxia.
MRI of the brain and spinal cord with gadolinium is the preferred imaging modality.
Cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands and elevated IgG synthesis rate and index are the most sensitive and specific tests.
Visual evoked potentials are possibly useful in diagnosing MS; however, its test properties (sensitivity 25%-83%; specificity 63%-88%) are limited.
Somatosensory evoked potentials also are possibly useful (sensitivity 14%-63%; specificity 40%-93%).
Visual evoked potentials may be needed to identify subclinical optic neuritis to fulfill diagnostic criteria for MS.

The diagnosis of MS rests on confirming that more than one area of the central nervous system is involved, known as "dissemination in space," and that the disease is an ongoing process, known as "dissemination in time."
Please see for a suggested approach to evaluation and management.
Interferon given to patients with a first attack of demyelinating disease reduces the likelihood of progression to multiple sclerosis (BENEFIT and CHAMPS studies). B
High dose vitamin D appears to reduce the likelihood of disease progression in patients with an initial episode (Clinically Isolated Syndrome or CIS).B
Acute attacks (episodes of neurologic dysfunction lasting greater than 24 hours) should be treated with high-dose oral or IV steroids for 3 to 5 days. A

Immunomodulatory medications such as monoclonal antibodies, interferons, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide, and glatiramer prevent relapses and slows disease progression in patients with relapsing remitting MS.A
Ocrelizumab is the only disease modifying agent shown to improve clinical outcomes in ambulatory patients with primary progressive MS.B
Tolebrutinib is effective for patients with secondary progressive MS.B

summarizes medications (including monoclonal antibodies) used for the treatment of MS. First-line therapy for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) includes injectable interferon beta or glatiramer acetate, and oral therapies like dimethyl fumarate or teriflunomide. Therapy with natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, or ublituximab reduces the likelihood of relapses in patients with relapsing forms of MS. Ocrelizumab is approved for primary progressive MS, and tolebrutinib is effective for secondary progressive MS.

Patients with Clinically Isolated Syndrome (n=316) suggestive of MS with vitamin D levels < 100 nmol/L were randomized to 100,000 IU oral cholecalciferol every two weeks or placebo. After 2 years, disease activity (clinical relapase and/or new MRI lesions) occurred less often in the vitamin D group (60% vs 74%, p =.004, NNT = 7). Secondary imaging related outcomes also favored the treatment group.
However, a similar study of 199 patients with CIS in Australia and New Zealand found no benefit in a similar population with daily doses ranging from 1000 to 10,000 IU of oral vitamin D3.

A trial randomized 89 participants with no relapses and no MRI activity over the previous 5 years to continuing or discontinuing disease modifying therapy. The trial was discontinued early because of inflammatory disease recurrence in the untreated group (18% vs 0%).

Discontinuation of natalizumab or fingolimod is associated with an increase in the risk of relapse, even in patients with stable disease on these medications. A French observational study used propensity score matching to compare patients over age 50 with no relapse or MRI change for at least 2 years who had discontinued highly effective therapy (fingolimod, natalizumab, or anti-CD20 therapy). Patients who discontinued fingolimod or natalizumab had a significant increase in risk of increased disease activity, but not following discontinuation of anti-CD20 therapies.

After 2 years, 45% of patients with Clinically Isolated Syndrome (CIS) suggestive of MS and with 2 or more clinically silent lesions on brain MRI who were treated with placebo developed clinically-definite MS compared with 28% in patients on interferon (NNT = 6) (BENEFIT trial). The benefits persisted after 3 years of follow-up. Similarly, 35% of patients with CIS receiving weekly doses of interferon beta-Ia developed clinically definite MS compared with 50% in those treated with placebo group (NNT = 7) (CHAMPS trial).

Patients treated with higher dose interferon have a lower rate of relapse than patients taking once-weekly interferon. However, interferon does not appear to prevent the development of permanent physical disability in slowly progressive MS.

Ocrelizumab is a monoclonal antibody that selectively depletes expression of CD20, a surface antigen of B cells. In an RCT with 732 patients with primary progressive MS, randomizing them in a 2:1 fashion to ocrelizumab or placebo, those assigned to ocrelizumab had somewhat less likelihood of progression at 24 weeks (30% vs. 36%, p = 0.04, NNT = 17). This was the prespecified primary endpoint, and at 120 weeks there was also somewhat less decrease in the timed 25 foot walk test. On the other hand, there was no difference over 2 years in physical function or quality of life scores, no difference in serious infections, but a non-significant increase in the likelihood of cancer (2.3% vs. 0.8%). A second RCT compared ocrelizumab with interferon beta-1a in a group of 1656 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis. The annual rate of relapse was significantly lower with active treatement (0.16 vs. 0.29 per year, p < 0.001, NNT = 8 to prevent one additional relapse per year). There was also a lower rate of disability progression at 24 weeks (6.9% vs. 10.5%, p = 0.003, NNT = 28). In this study, there was no difference in the likelihood of neoplasia or serious infections.

Ublituximab is a CD20 targetting monoclonal antibody approved for treatment of relapsing remitting MS and clinically isolated syndrome. In a trial randomizing 545 patients to ublituximab or teriflunomide, after 96 weeks there significantly fewer CNS lesions in the ublituximab group and a lower relapse rate, but no difference in disability progression. Adverse reactions were more common with ublitusimab.

Alemtuzumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to a surface protein of mature lymphocytes (CD52), targeting them for destruction. Among 581 patients with a relatively new diagnosis of relapsing-remitting MS and previously untreated (except with corticosteroids), alemtuzumab (Lemtrada) was more effective in 2-year disease free intervals compared to with interferon beta-1a (74% vs. 56%). However, disability rates were similar in both groups. Among patients with established disease despite treatment, alemtuzumab also prevented relapse in 65% of patients compared with 47% in the interferon group, and decreased disability in this group. Side effects were common including herpes infections (~18% in both groups). It is approved in Europe but not in the U.S. for MS.

Patients with relapsing MS treated with the combination of natalizumab and interferon experienced fewer relapses (0.34 per year) compared with patients treated with interferon alone (0.75 per year). Adverse events associated with combination therapy were anxiety, pharyngitis, sinus congestion, and peripheral edema. However, the risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is higher in patients with a positive John Cunningham virus antibody, and is contraindicated in these patients. It is a restricted drug that can only be prescribed by physicians, infusion centers, and pharmacies enrolled in an FDA approved program through the manufacturer.

A RCT identified 1131 patients with nonrelapsing secondary progressive MS and randomized them 2:1 to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor tolebrutinib or placebo. At 2.5 years, patients in the treatment group were less likely to have sustained disability progression (22.6% vs 30.7%, p = .003, NNT = 12). Serious adverse events were more common with treatment (15% vs 10%, NNH = 20).

Two RCTs (n= 975 and n=889) randomized patients with relapsing MS to toletrunib or teriflunomide in a 1:1 ratio. After approximately 2.5 years of follow-up there was no significant difference between groups in annual relpase rates (0.13 vs 0.12 and 0.11 vs 0.11). In a post hoc analysis toletrunib was associated with a lower rate of confirmed disability for 6 or more months (8.3% v 11.3%).
In a phase 2 trial with 166 participants, the anti-CD40L monoclonal antibody frexalimab reduced the number of new gadolinium enhancing lesions on MRI. Further clinical trials are needed.

Daclizumab is another monoclonal antibody that binds CD52. However, based on 2 trials with 851 patients a Cochrane review concluded that there was insufficient evidence to determine whether it was more effective than placebo.
There is insufficient evidence regarding the efficacy of the monoclonal antibody rituximab in relapsing-remitting MS.

Patients with relapses affecting function treated with high-dose IV steroids (e.g., 1000 mg IV methylprednisolone daily for 3-5 days) have faster recovery of neurologic symptoms than those treated with placebo. There is limited evidence on the effectiveness of long-term corticosteroids.

In an analysis of 215 patients from 5 studies with MS relapses randomized to either oral corticosteroids or IV corticosteroids, no significant differences were noted in relapse recovery at week four, nor differences in MRI gadolinium enhancement activity.
Spasticity: While spasticity is an important problem, the effectiveness of medications such as (baclofen, dantrolene, and tizanidine) has not been well-studied in MS.

Urinary incontinence: Medication options for urinary incontinence include anticholinergics (such as oxybutynin and tolterodine) and imipramine; however, they are limited by side effects such as dry mouth. A recent Cochrane review concluded that the there is insufficient evidence supporting the use of anticholinergic drugs for frequency, urgeny or incontinence in patients with MS, and that a 20% withdrawal rate is associated with their use in clnical trials.
Neuropathic pain: Options to treat neuropathic pain include gabapentin, carbamazepine, pregabalin, and duloxetine.

Diroximel fumarate has the same active metabolite as dimethyl fumarate and is approved for relapsing remitting MS and clinically isolated syndrome. It has better GI tolerability than dimethyl fumarate. A Cochrane review identified 2 RCTs of dimethyl fumarate and concluded that it reduced the number of patients with a relapse (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.66) or disability worsening (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.87) over two years compared to placebo.

Teriflunomide 7 mg to 14 mg is approved for clinically isolated syndrome and relapsing remitting MS. A systematic review of 5 RCTs with 3231 patients concluded that there was low-quality evidence that teriflunomide 7 mg to 14 mg/day reduces the likelihood of relapse (RR 0.60 to 0.72). The higher dose may prevent progression of disability based on very low quality evidence.
Over a 2 year period, patients with relapsing remitting MS treated with glatiramer (co-polymer 1) had an average of 0.6 relapses per year compared with 0.8 for those treated with placebo.

Among 221 patients in 3 trials, mitoxantrone reduced the progression of disability at 2-years compared to placebo (or placebo and steroids) by 70%, as well as the relapse rate and the number of patients with active MRI lesions. However, post-marketing data have found high rates of cardiomyopathy, ovarian failure, male infertility, promyelocytic leukemia, and chromosomal aberrations. In general, it would not be used for treatment of MS.
A recent Cochrane review concluded that "weak and inconclusive evidence" exists for amantadine, pemoline and modafinil for the for the treatment of fatigue in MS patients receiving palliative care.

Among 142 patient's with a first demyelinating event (mean age 35.8 years, 68.3% women), 72 patient's randomized to 100 mg of minocycline given twice daily or less likely to convert to multiple sclerosis within 6 months of randomization compared with those randomized to placebo (70 patients; 61% and the placebo group versus 33.4% in the minocycline group); however there was no difference between the 2 groups after 24 month.

Statins are not effective for MS, based on 4 trials with 458 persons. A single trial in 140 patients found that high dose simvastatin reduced the rate of brain atrophy, but the clinical significance of this is unknown.

Fingolimiod is an oral sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator. In an RCT with 215 patients age 10 to 17 years with relapsing MS, those randomized to fingolimod had fewer relapses per year (0.12 vs. 0.67 with interferon beta, p < 0.001) and fewer MRI lesions. However, serious adverse events were more common in the active treatment group (16.8% vs. 6.5% in the interferon group).

Surgical options are available for managing medication-refractory spasticity include intrathecal baclofen pump placement and tendon-release surgery. Intrathecal baclofen is more useful for lower extremity spasticity when oral baclofen cannot be tolerated at high doses.
Small studies have found that botulinum toxin injections to be better than placebo at improving spasticity.
For chronic urinary incontinence in patients unable to self-catheterize, placement of a suprapubic catheter should be considered.
A single intrasphincteric injection of boulinum toxin was no better than placebo in decreasing post-voiding residual urine in patients with MS.
While many complimentary and alternative medicine approaches are anecdotally suggested to be beneficial for MS, no controlled trials have demonstrated any impact on the course of the disease.
Patients participating in yoga in an exercise class had comparable improvements in fatigue and energy while control patients on a waiting list did not.

While anecdotal reports suggested that cannabinoids might help improve spasticity, a systematic review found mixed evidence, with one high quality trial finding improvement in spasticity compared to placebo, but two lower quality trials finding no benefit. Specifically this review evaluated medical marijuana on several outcomes in patients with MS. A single high quality study found no effect on spacticity, and no effect on bladder symptoms or incontinence; although in several lower quality studites, the results for these outcomes were mixed. For central pain in patients with MS, the single high quality trial found marijuana superior to placebo.
Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) have no major effect on disease progression in MS, and neither did vitamin supplementation (including vitamin D).

In 9 small randomized studies, exercise therapy appears to benefit patients with MS not having an exacerbation, with a 5% to 36% improvement in muscle strength and a 21% improvement in functional capacity in patients with MS.

Progressive aerobic exercise (PAE) for 24 weeks was not associated with a "neuroprotective evffect" as measured by brain volume change, however it was assocaited with cardiorespiratory fitness and lower relapse rates among patients with MS.
Short term multidisciplinary rehabilitation programs improve function after a relapse of MS, however there are no data on the long-term effectiveness.
Data on the effectiveness of occupational therapy and vocal rehabilitation is limited.
Multiple sclerosis is associated with high rates of mood disorders, particularly depression.
Antidepressants and cognitive behavioral therapy improve depression scores in patients with MS-related depression.

The wide range of psychological interventions in patients with MS makes it difficult to assign a net effect. Nonetheless, in controlled studies cognitive behavioral approaches are beneficial in treating depression and in helping patients cope and adjust to a new diagnosis of MS.

A Cochrane review concluded that there was low level evidence for the benefit of neuropsychological/cognitive rehabilitation in patients with MS, based on 20 studies with 986 participants. Improvements were seen in memory and attention, primarily.
Another Cochrane review concluded based on 4 studies that memory rehabilitation improves some outcomes in patients with MS.

There is no evidence from controlled trials to show that certain foods, diets, or vitamin supplementation alter disease course or prevent its onset. Omega-6 fatty acids show some promise but data are insufficient to draw firm conclusions.
Hyperbaric oxygen is ineffective.

In a phase 2 singlearm trial in patients with multiple sclerosis aged 18 to 50 years old, with a poor prognosis, autologous stem cell transplantation was associated with multiple sclerosis activity free survival 3 years after transplantation and 69.6% of patient's and no new gadolinium enhanced lesions or new T2 lesions on MRI sequential scanning in the absence of disease-modifying drugs.

In a randomized controlled trial of 110 patient's with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis, hematopoietic stem cell transplant was associated with a significantly prolonged time to disease progression, and improved scores on the expanded disability status scale after a mean follow up of 2.8 years compared to traditional disease modifying therapy.
While patients should be treated for life, there is no consensus on what constitutes a "treatment failure" and what warrants changing a patient's medication.
Patients with MS should be referred to a neurologist for management.
Patients with acute exacerbations may require hospitalization when IV steroids cannot be given at home or in the outpatient setting.
Hospitalize patients with severe exacerbations causing acute disability for monitoring and subsequent rehabilitation.
Medical complications of advanced MS include infections such as aspiration pneumonia that require IV antibiotics.
Similarly, MS patients with dysphagia who are unable to meet fluid and nutrition needs may need inpatient stabilization.
Referral to social workers, wound care specialists, urologists, and physiatrists may also be warranted.
MS is both highly variable and unpredictable in its course. The majority of patients begin with relapsing-remitting MS and 50% ultimately convert to secondary progressive disease. B
In the first year after diagnosis, older age, greater disability and pyramidal signs (e.g., spasicity and weakness) represent early indicators of aggressive MS.
Two months after relapses, even when treated, at least 25% have moderate residual effects and about 40% have mild residual effects. B
About 17% of patients have a benign course without developing significant disability. B
The majority of untreated patients will develop some degree of neurologic dysfunction, and disease-modifying therapies decrease this risk. A
Data on the natural-history of MS pre-dates the introduction of medications for MS, which first became approved in 1993.
The majority of patients (85% of patients in one series) initially present with relapsing remitting MS. About 50% of untreated patients ultimately progress to secondary progressive MS.
A substantial proportion of patients (17%) have benign MS. These patients have low disability scores and have a greater than 90% chance of remaining stable for 10 years.
MS can cause various debilitating symptoms which can include, spasticity, urinary incontinence, and neuropathic pain.
Untreated patients will develop some degree of neurologic dysfunction. About 50% of patients will require assistance to walk 15 years after diagnosis.

Patients with MS experience many complications of disability and immobility: urinary tract infection, aspiration pneumonia, spastic limb contractures, and the presence of pressure ulcers and deep vein thromboses in the wheelchair- and bed-confined patients.
Despite the accrual of disability, MS is not considered a fatal disease: 76% of patients were found to be alive at 25 years after diagnosis compared with 88% of patients without MS.

In a systemic review (12 studies, 1524 patients) of urinary retention (greater than 300 mL) in MS patients, it was noted that 53% of MS patients have detrusor overactivity, 43% have detrusor sphincter dyssynergia, and 12% have atonic bladder as the cause of retention.
MS is highly variable and unpredictable in its course. Most cases begin as relapsing-remitting MS, and 50% ultimately convert to secondary progressive disease.
Two months after relapses, even when treated, at least 25% have moderate residual effects and about 40% have mild residual effects.

The following are associated with poor short-term prognosis: older age of onset, male gender, African-American ethnicity, motor or cerebellar symptoms, short interval between first and second attacks, and incomplete recovery from initial attack. About 25% of patients with 4 or more of these risk factors had progression of disease compared with 17% of those with none of just 1.
Newly-diagnosed patients should be seen every 3 months during the first year.

Treatment with interferon beta is associated with developing neutralizing antibodies. However, there is insufficient data on the clinical utility of neutralizing antibodies, and therefore caution should be exercised when applying results on treatment decisions.
None of the current disease modifying drugs available are FDA approved for use in pregnancy.
In animal studies, interferons were linked with a higher rate of miscarriages.
Glatiramer acetate is pregnancy category C: it has not been demonstrated to have adverse effects on the fetus, although its use during pregnancy confers an unknown degree of risk.

In a study where the annual prepregnancy rate of relapse was 0.7 per year, the rate of relapse during pregnancy progressively decreased (0.5 per year during first trimester; 0.6 during second trimester and 0.2 during the third trimester).
The rate of relapse, however, increased to 1.2 during the first three months post-partum.

cell.label: Patient with neurologic symptoms. Hyperacute onset (seconds to minutes).
Workup for other causes. Initially stroke, seizure, or migraine. If negative, consider neoplastic, infectious; see Differential Diagnosis section.
Localization to brain (unilateral weakness, vision, brainstem signs) or spinal cord (bilateral extremity weakness, sensory level, bowel/bladder)?
Order other scan (brain or spinal cord). Apply McDonald criteria ().
Lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands, IgG index, IgG synthesis rate, and cell counts.
cell.path: Positive oligoclonal bands, IgG index, or IgG synthesis rate
Normal; repeat brain MRI in 3 months

cell.label: Interval new lesions meeting McDonald criteria?
Repeat brain MRI in 6 months and reassess for interval new lesions.
Consider starting disease-modifying agents including minocycline ().
MRI of cervical and thoracic spine. Demyelinating lesions?

Disease-Modifying Agent FDA-Approved Indication Dose/Route Frequency Comment
Glatiramer acetate (Copaxone) RRMS 20 mg subcutaneously Daily None
Interferon beta-1a (Avonex) RRMS, CIS 30 mcg IM Weekly Monitor LFTs/CBC every 3 months
Interferon beta-1a (Rebif) RRMS 44 mcg subcutaneously TIW Monitor LFTs/CBC every 3 months
Interferon beta-1b (Betaseron) RRMS, CIS 250 mcg subcutaneously Every other day Monitor LFTs/CBC every 3 months
Natalizumab (Tysabri) RRMS,inadequate responseto other DMAs 300 mg IV Monthly Drug is restricted to registered prescribers, infusion centers, and pharmacies. Do not give to patients with John Cunning virus antibodies, due to increased risk of PML.
Ocrelizumab (Ocrevus) RRMS or PPMS 300 mg to 600 mg IV Every 6 months Initial dose is 300 mg repeated 2 weeks later; subsequent doses 600 mg
Fingolimod (Gilenya) RRMS 0.5 mg by mouth mulonce daily Once daily Take with or without food. First dose monitoring for bradycardia. Contraindicated with known CV recent CV events or history of arrhythmias.
Alemtuzumab (Lemtrada) RRMS 12 mg IV infusion over 5 days, followed by 3 day infusion 12 months later Generally reserved for patients with an inadequate response to two or more previous drugs, due to poor safety profile.
Teriflunomide (Aubagio) CIS, RRMS 7 to 14 mg orally Once daily Obtain transaminase and bilirubin levels within 6 months before initiation of the drug. Monitor ALT levels at least monthly for six months after starting teriflunomide.
Ublituximab (Briumvi) CIS, RRMS 150 mg infusion (initial dose) and 450 mg infusion (subsequent doses) Initial dose, then 2 weeks later, then every 24 weeks Careful monitoring for hepatitis B and avaoidance of live vaccines. See prescribing information for detailed guidance.
Tolebrutinib SPMS 60 mg once daily Once daily NNT = 12 for disease progression, NNH = 20 for serious AEs.
High dose vitamin D CIS 100,000 IU oral cholecalciferol Every 2 weeks Reduced progression on MRI or relapse (NNT = 7)
Abbreviations: FDA, Food and Drug Administration; RRMS, relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis; PPMS, primary progressive multiple sclerosis; CIS, clinically isolated syndrome; DMA, disease-modifying agent; SPMS, secondary progressive multiple sclerosis; LFTs, liver function tests.
